finder.title: Find the right solution
finder.subtitle: Answer three quick questions. Each step adapts to the previous one, and the result shows only the products that fit.
finder.s1_help: Pick every place you run things. The next step only shows what applies to your picks.
finder.s2_help: Only the services of the environments you picked are listed. Select what you use today.
finder.s3_title: What do you want to solve?
finder.s3_help: Pick one or more goals, or let us suggest. Goals that do not fit your selection are listed below with what would enable them.
finder.none_in_step: Nothing selected in this step yet. You can skip it.
finder.so_far_empty: Your recommendation builds up as you select.
finder.result_based_one: Based on the {{count}} item you selected.
finder.result_based_other: Based on the {{count}} items you selected.
finder.coverage_gap: Items marked "Not covered" have no recommendation on this site yet; use the contact option to talk about them.
finder.path_lead: Read from the top: overviews first, then one page per item, then capabilities.
finder.empty_result_desc: Answer at least one question to see which products fit your environment.

why.sm: Workloads, pipelines and scripts get secrets at run time with a platform-attested identity, so nothing stays hardcoded.
why.swa: Workloads prove who they are with short-lived SPIFFE IDs (SVIDs) and use them for mTLS, cloud federation or secret exchange.
why.cp: Applications that consume privileged accounts from PAM fetch them at run time, with a local cache and rotation handled by the CPM.
why.shub: Secrets stay where developers already read them (cloud stores and HashiCorp Vault) while PAM keeps rotation and audit.

finder.note_iot: The general approaches below (client certificate or API key authentication) are a starting point; validate the device constraints with the team.
finder.other_desc: Describe your environment and we will point you to the right integration.
finder.starting_point: Recommendations are a starting point, not a sizing. Check each page for availability and limitations, or
finder.compare_link: compare the options side by side.

reason.k8sArch: Pods prove who they are with their Kubernetes identity (JWT); start here to see the options.
reason.sdk: The app authenticates and fetches secrets itself with the SDK.
reason.sidecar: The Secrets Provider sidecar delivers secrets with no vault code in the app.
reason.eso: External Secrets Operator syncs secrets into Kubernetes Secrets.
reason.csi: Secrets Store CSI Driver mounts secrets as a volume.
reason.spmodes: Secrets Provider as init container, sidecar or push-to-file.
reason.reloader: Restarts pods when a secret changes.
reason.secretless: The app connects through a local broker and never sees the database credential (Self-Hosted).
reason.jenkins: The plugin authenticates with a short-lived Jenkins-signed JWT.
reason.gitlab: Each job authenticates with its GitLab ID token (JWT).
reason.azdo: The extension authenticates with the Entra ID token of a service connection.
reason.gha: Workflows use the GitHub OIDC token: no credential stored in GitHub.
reason.bitbucket: Each step authenticates with its Bitbucket OIDC token.
reason.circleci: The orb trades the CircleCI OIDC token for secrets.
reason.octopus: A step template fetches secrets with an OIDC token.
reason.ansible: A lookup plugin resolves secrets at play time.
reason.terraform: The provider reads secrets; ephemeral forms keep them out of the state.
reason.puppet: A Deferred lookup lets the agent fetch the secret with its own identity (Self-Hosted).
reason.cf: Service Broker and buildpack deliver secrets to apps (Self-Hosted).
reason.mulesoft: The Mule connector retrieves secrets in flows.
reason.python: Python SDK, including the AWS IAM client for Lambda.
reason.awsIam: Workloads on AWS authenticate with their IAM role.
reason.azureMi: Workloads on Azure authenticate with a managed identity.
reason.gcpId: Workloads on Google Cloud authenticate with the metadata identity token.
reason.dynamic: Just-in-time cloud credentials with a TTL (AWS; GCP on SaaS).
reason.apiKey: Hosts without a platform identity authenticate with an API key.
reason.cert: mTLS with a client certificate proves the workload.
reason.summon: Injects secrets as environment variables into a process.
reason.rotation: How passwords rotate in each edition.
reason.mcp: AI coding tools create secrets and workloads through MCP (SaaS, beta).
reason.swaArch: SPIFFE SVIDs issued after attestation replace static secrets.
reason.swaS3: An SVID is exchanged for AWS STS credentials: no static keys.
reason.swaAi: JWT-SVIDs replace API keys for AI agents (SaaS).
reason.cpAgent: An agent on the host serves passwords from an encrypted cache.
reason.ascp: Data sources get credentials at runtime with no code change.
reason.ccp: Central REST web service: no agent on the application host.
reason.zos: Batch jobs get passwords at runtime instead of JCL or datasets.
reason.dual: Two accounts alternate so rotation causes no downtime.
reason.shubPc: Keeps cloud secret stores in sync with Privilege Cloud, no app change.
reason.shubSh: Same sync with PAM Self-Hosted 11.5 or later as the source.
reason.audit: Every authentication and secret fetch leaves an audit event you can send to your SIEM.

finder.prereq_lead: What must be ready before each integration: prerequisites, network rules (numbers are the flows in the diagram and network table) and the official documentation for each item.
finder.prereq_see_page: No prerequisites beyond the general product items.
finder.prereq_shared: Items used by more than one integration, listed once.
finder.report_sources: Recommendations are a starting point, not sizing. Check availability and limitations in the official documentation listed under each item before planning.

sm: An IDIRA Secrets Manager SaaS tenant or a Self-Hosted cluster; on SaaS, workloads live under the data/ branch.
Workloads and pipelines can reach the Secrets Manager API over HTTPS (TCP 443).
An admin who can load policy and create or enable authenticators (SaaS: Authn_Admins or Conjur_Cloud_Admins).
Secrets Manager CLI v9.x for the setup steps.
swa: Secure Workload Access is available in the US-EAST-1 region only.
TCP 8443 on the SWA Server reachable from every node or VM that runs an agent.
Secret permissions granted to new workload identities before they need secrets.
cp: PAM Self-Hosted (Digital Vault 14.0 or later) or Privilege Cloud.
An administrative Vault or Privilege Cloud user for the installation.
The provider user in every password Safe with List, Retrieve and View Safe Members; the application needs List and Retrieve.
shub: Privilege Cloud, or PAM Self-Hosted 11.5 or later through a connector, as the source.
Up to 5 connectors per tenant; connector host on Windows Server 2016 to 2025 with 8 cores and 8 GB RAM.
Only secrets are synced (no keys, certificates or dual accounts), in one direction.

k8sArch: SaaS: the Kubernetes integration uses the JWT authenticator (authn-jwt); certificate-based authn-k8s is Self-Hosted only.
Setup needs a Secrets Manager admin and a Kubernetes cluster admin, plus Secrets Manager CLI v9 or later.
sdk: Java 8 or later with Spring Boot 2.x or 3.x.
Spring Cloud 2021.x or 2022.x for external property configuration.
A JWT authenticator for the cluster, or API key authentication (a secret zero to protect).
sidecar: Secrets Provider for Kubernetes added as a sidecar in the application Pod.
A JWT authenticator configured for the cluster.
Containers that read environment variables see a new value only after a restart: plan Reloader or mounted files.
eso: External Secrets Operator installed in the cluster.
Kubernetes 1.22 or later when the service account JWT comes from the TokenRequest API.
The JWT must be compatible with the configured JWT authenticator.
csi: Secrets Store CSI Driver installed with Helm (a DaemonSet on every node).
The CSIDriver tokenRequests audience set to conjur.
Secrets Manager CLI v9.x installed and logged in.
spmodes: Choose init container, sidecar, Job or standalone: only the sidecar and standalone update after start.
Push-to-File works only with the init container and the sidecar.
Fetch all: at most 500 secrets; keep the host scoped to one app (least privilege).
reloader: Secrets Provider Helm chart in application or standalone mode.
Workloads that reference the Secret directly (envFrom, secretKeyRef or volume).
Application mode: an external trigger such as a CronJob to rerun the Job.
secretless: Secrets Manager Self-Hosted (Secretless is not documented for SaaS).
A Follower with the Kubernetes Authenticator in the cluster.
A target with a supported connector (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MSSQL, SSH, HTTP).
Secretless listening only on localhost, or a Unix socket protected by OS permissions.
jenkins: The Jenkins secrets plugin installed by an administrator, followed by a Jenkins restart.
Jenkins 2.455 or later for the current plugin.
JWT or API key authentication set up in Secrets Manager for the jobs.
gha: A workflow allowed to request an OIDC token (permissions: id-token: write).
Secrets Manager CLI installed and logged in for the setup.
Docker for Linux and a self-hosted GitHub runner, as listed in the system requirements.
ansible: The Secrets Manager Ansible collection, which includes the lookup plugin.
An identity for the control node (API key or a supported authenticator).
Ansible files set to minimum permissions.
terraform: Ephemeral resources (Terraform 1.10+) or write-only arguments (1.11+) to keep secrets out of state; protect the state file anyway.
api_key outside the .tf file (environment or sensitive variables).
JWT mode: host_id when the authenticator lacks token-app-property and identity-path.
gitlab: Docker, Go 1.20.2+, GitLab 15.11.2+, GitLab Runner 15.8.2+ and Secrets Manager CLI v9.x.
Runner images based on Alpine, Ubuntu or UBI-FIPS.
ID token aud equal to the authenticator audience.
Admin rights to create the JWT authenticator.
azdo: An Azure identity (managed identity or app registration) and an Azure Resource Manager service connection.
secrets.yml in the repository that triggers the pipeline.
Service ID with the authenticator name only (azure-devops).
bitbucket: A Bitbucket Cloud repository and a step with oidc: true.
Workload name and annotation equal to the repository UUID, braces included.
Delete secrets.env afterwards if you do not use load_secrets.sh.
circleci: Audience set to your CircleCI organization ID.
The workload sub annotation matching the full sub claim.
The PEM certificate when Secrets Manager uses a self-signed certificate.
octopus: A Generic OIDC account with audience conjur.
Workload name and sub annotation equal to the sub claim.
Every mapped secret accessible: one missing secret fails the step.
python: The AWS IAM client installed from the GitHub source (git clone and pip3 install).
Call create_conjur_iam_client again after five to eight minutes (no token refresh).
cf: Secrets Manager Self-Hosted (there is no SaaS page).
Ops Manager v2.7 to v3.0 and TAS v4, v5, v6 or 10.2; cf CLI newer than 6.38 for multiple buildpacks.
One service instance per space and a dedicated policy branch for the broker host.
puppet: Secrets Manager Self-Hosted (there is no SaaS page).
A host API key on each node, protected and rotated.
Secrets resolved with Deferred so they stay out of the catalog, PuppetDB and reports.
mulesoft: An API key kept in secure properties and rotated.
At least one certificate file (.pem or .der) for Edge (SaaS) or Self-Hosted.
awsIam: Workload ID exactly AccountID/RoleName of the AWS resource.
The documented STS permission on the IAM role (SaaS).
SigV4 signing region matching the STS endpoint (us-east-1 for the global endpoint).
azureMi: A supported service: Virtual Machines, App Services, Functions or Container Instances.
Subscription ID and resource group annotations on every host.
provider-uri set and the authenticator enabled before workloads authenticate.
gcpId: Identity token audience equal to the full host ID; on Compute Engine request format=full.
Only one GCP authenticator can be configured.
dynamic: An issuer created by a Secrets Manager admin, and membership in its consumers group.
A long-lived IAM user key or GCP service account key for the issuer, kept in PAM with rotation.
Dynamic secrets under data/dynamic, with a TTL between 900 and 43,200 seconds.
apiKey: The API key stored and protected like a password: it is a secret zero.
A manual rotation plan that replaces the key everywhere it is used.
The login URL-encoded in the request path.
cert: SaaS: certificate authentication works only toward a Secrets Manager Edge.
A PEM CA bundle with exactly one root CA.
At least one annotation (san-uri, san-dns, san-ip or cn) and the authenticator enabled.
summon: Summon installed from its GitHub repository (it is versioned on its own).
An identity already configured on the machine (CLI login, host API key or another method).
execute or update privilege on every variable listed in secrets.yml.
rotation: SaaS: secrets rotate only when they come from PAM.
Self-Hosted local rotation: AWS access keys and PostgreSQL only; enable it again after Leader upgrades and failover.
Applications that read the secret again on authentication errors, or dual accounts.
mcp: Development environments only (not supported in production).
A dedicated user for the AI tool: the agent reaches every secret that user can reach.
The generated .env with the workload API key kept out of version control.
swaArch: RSA signing on the trust domain when secrets are exchanged (the JWT authenticator accepts RSA only).
k8s_psat needs network access from the SWA Server to the Kubernetes API server; otherwise use k8s_jwt.
bootstrap.bundleSourceUrl set, or a manual agent restart after a server CA rotation.
swaS3: For AWS federation, the issuer URL must be a public, unauthenticated HTTPS URL.
An IAM OIDC provider and role that trust the SWA issuer.
swaAi: JWT-SVIDs for Claude API federation (X.509 SVIDs cannot be exchanged).
The issuer URL registered with Anthropic matching the iss claim exactly.
Gemini Enterprise: the SWA server exposed with a LoadBalancer service (gRPC on 8443).
The Workload API socket and token files protected.
cpAgent: A supported OS (for example RHEL, Ubuntu, AIX or Windows Server 2016 to 2025).
Application Password SDKs on the same machine and at the same version as the CP.
The application OS user with read and write on /tmp or the folder set in AIM_TEMP_FOLDER.
ascp: A supported Credential Provider on the same machine (ASCP is an add-on).
JRE 1.8.x or higher on Linux, Windows or AIX; IPv4 only.
Application server, data source and database listed in the support table.
ccp: Windows with IIS 10 (IIS 6 compatibility), ASP.NET 4.x and ISAPI.
IIS hardening done by the customer.
Behind a load balancer: X-Forwarded-For with TrustedProxies, or certificate pass-through.
zos: z/OS 2.5, 3.1 or 3.2 with IBM Java 8, SMP/E V3R6 or later, IBM XML Toolkit V1.11 and JZOS.
One provider per LPAR, its STC under a UID 0 user, IPv4 only.
z/OS and Vault clocks synchronized to UTC (for example with NTP).
shubPc: A Privilege Cloud tenant as the source.
Azure Key Vault on the RBAC permission model (Access policy vaults are not supported).
Secret names within store limits (AWS up to 512 characters, Azure up to 127).
shubSh: PAM Self-Hosted 11.5 or later reaching Secrets Hub through a connector.
Connector host on Windows Server 2016 to 2025 with 8 cores, 8 GB RAM and 500 MB disk.
Write access to synced secrets restricted in the target (sync is one-way).

finder.s2_empty_desc: This step lists the services of each environment you pick in step 1.

unsure.name: Not sure, suggest for me
unsure.help: We pick goals from what you selected.

hardcoded.name: Remove hardcoded secrets
hardcoded.help: Apps, scripts and pipelines fetch secrets at run time instead of storing them.
hardcoded.needs: Add a workload, server, pipeline or app in step 2.

vault_gov.name: Govern cloud vaults from PAM
vault_gov.help: Keep AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager or HashiCorp Vault, with rotation and audit from PAM.
vault_gov.needs: Add a cloud secret store or HashiCorp Vault in step 2.

legacy_pam.name: Legacy apps get credentials from PAM
legacy_pam.help: Servers, app servers, legacy apps and mainframe jobs fetch privileged accounts from PAM.
legacy_pam.needs: Add servers, app servers, legacy apps or mainframe in step 2.

workload_id.name: Workload identity without secrets
workload_id.help: SPIFFE identities for mTLS, cloud federation and secret exchange.
workload_id.needs: Add Kubernetes or virtual machines in step 2.

ai.name: Secure AI agents
ai.help: Agents and AI tools work without long-lived keys in code or config.
ai.needs: Add AI agents or assistants in step 1.

dynamic.name: Short-lived cloud credentials
dynamic.help: Just-in-time AWS or Google Cloud credentials that expire on their own.
dynamic.needs: Add an AWS or Google Cloud service in step 2.

rotation.name: Rotation without downtime
rotation.help: Rotate passwords without breaking the apps that use them.
rotation.needs: Add servers, databases, legacy apps or a cloud store in step 2.

audit.name: Audit and compliance
audit.help: Know which workload accessed which secret, and when.

needs_pam.cp: Credential Providers need PAM Self-Hosted (Digital Vault 14.0 or later) or Privilege Cloud. Add the PAM you have in step 1 to tailor the result.
needs_pam.shub: Secrets Hub needs Privilege Cloud, or PAM Self-Hosted 11.5 or later through a connector, as the source. Add the PAM you have in step 1 to tailor the result.

info.recommend_none: Nothing on the site maps to this item yet.
info.note_sh_only: Documented for Secrets Manager Self-Hosted only.
info.note_secretless: Secretless Broker is documented for Secrets Manager Self-Hosted only.
info.note_pam_cp: Credential Providers work with both PAM back ends (PAM Self-Hosted and Privilege Cloud).

aws.what: Workloads running on Amazon Web Services: virtual machines, functions, containers and the AWS secret store.
signs: Your apps run on EC2, Lambda, EKS or ECS.
You already keep secrets in AWS Secrets Manager.
aws.includes: EC2, Lambda, EKS, ECS / Fargate, AWS Secrets Manager

azure.what: Workloads and tools on Microsoft Azure: virtual machines, AKS, App Service and Functions, Azure DevOps pipelines and Key Vault.
signs: Your apps run on Azure VMs, AKS or App Service.
Your pipelines run in Azure DevOps or you use Azure Key Vault.
azure.includes: Virtual Machines, AKS, App Service / Functions, Azure DevOps, Azure Key Vault

gcp.what: Workloads on Google Cloud: Compute Engine, GKE, Cloud Run and Cloud Functions, and GCP Secret Manager.
signs: Your apps run on Compute Engine, GKE or Cloud Run.
You already keep secrets in GCP Secret Manager.
gcp.includes: Compute Engine, GKE, Cloud Run / Functions, GCP Secret Manager

k8s.what: Kubernetes clusters you run yourself or on premises, including OpenShift. Managed clusters (EKS, AKS, GKE) are under each cloud.
signs: You deploy containers with Kubernetes or OpenShift.
Pods need database passwords, API tokens or certificates.
k8s.includes: OpenShift, other distributions (Rancher, Tanzu Kubernetes, vanilla and others)

onprem.what: Your own data center: Linux and Windows servers, app servers, packaged or legacy apps, databases, Cloud Foundry, HashiCorp Vault and devices.
signs: You run servers or VMs in your own data center.
Legacy apps or app servers still keep passwords in files.
onprem.includes: Linux and Windows servers, app servers, legacy apps, Cloud Foundry / Tanzu, databases, HashiCorp Vault, IoT devices

mainframe.what: IBM z/OS batch jobs and programs that need passwords for databases or other systems.
signs: JCL jobs or programs on z/OS use stored passwords.
You want those passwords to come from PAM and rotate.
mainframe.includes: z/OS batch, JCL, programs that call the SDK

cicd.what: Pipelines and automation tools that need credentials to build, test and deploy.
signs: Pipelines keep secrets in CI variables or in the repository.
Automation (Ansible, Terraform, Puppet) needs credentials to reach systems.
cicd.includes: Jenkins, GitLab, GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, Bitbucket, CircleCI, Octopus Deploy, Ansible, Terraform, Puppet

ai.what: AI agents and AI coding assistants that call APIs or need secrets to do their work.
signs: You build or run AI agents that call other services.
Developers use AI assistants that create or read secrets.
ai.includes: AI agents (custom, Claude, Gemini Enterprise), AI coding assistants that use MCP

pam.what: The privileged access management you already have. It is the source for Secrets Hub and the back end for Credential Providers.
signs: You already use Privilege Cloud or PAM Self-Hosted.
Privileged accounts are stored in Safes and rotated by the CPM.

other.what: Something that is not on the list. Tell us about it and we will point you to the right integration.
signs: Your platform or tool is not listed here.
You are not sure where your case fits.

aws_ec2.what: Virtual machines on AWS. They can prove who they are with their IAM role.
signs: Apps or scripts run on EC2 instances.
Instances read credentials from files or environment variables.

aws_lambda.what: Serverless functions on AWS that run with an IAM execution role.
signs: You run Lambda functions that call databases or APIs.
Function settings hold passwords or tokens.

aws_eks.what: Managed Kubernetes on AWS. Pods prove who they are with the cluster service account token.
signs: You run workloads on Amazon EKS.
Pods use Kubernetes Secrets or files with credentials.

aws_ecs.what: Containers on Amazon ECS or Fargate, running with an IAM task role.
signs: You run containers on ECS or Fargate.
Task definitions carry passwords or tokens.

aws_sm.what: The AWS secret store. Developers read secrets there with the native AWS SDK.
signs: Your apps already read secrets from AWS Secrets Manager.
You want PAM rotation and audit without changing those apps.

az_vm.what: Virtual machines on Azure. They can prove who they are with a managed identity.
signs: Apps or scripts run on Azure VMs.
VMs read credentials from files or environment variables.

az_aks.what: Managed Kubernetes on Azure. Pods prove who they are with the cluster service account token.
signs: You run workloads on AKS.
Pods use Kubernetes Secrets or files with credentials.

az_app.what: Azure App Service and Azure Functions, which can use a managed identity.
signs: Web apps or functions run on App Service or Functions.
App settings hold connection strings or keys.

azdo.what: Azure DevOps pipelines. The same item appears under Azure and under CI/CD.
signs: Your builds and releases run in Azure DevOps.
Pipelines keep secrets in variable groups or service connections.

az_kv.what: The Azure secret store. Developers read secrets there with the native Azure SDK.
signs: Your apps already read secrets from Azure Key Vault.
You want PAM rotation and audit without changing those apps.

gcp_ce.what: Virtual machines on Google Cloud, running with a service account.
signs: Apps or scripts run on Compute Engine.
VMs read credentials from files or metadata.

gcp_gke.what: Managed Kubernetes on Google Cloud. Pods prove who they are with the cluster service account token.
signs: You run workloads on GKE.
Pods use Kubernetes Secrets or files with credentials.

gcp_run.what: Cloud Run services and Cloud Functions, running with a service account.
signs: You run containers on Cloud Run or functions on Cloud Functions.
Their settings hold passwords or tokens.

gcp_sm.what: The Google Cloud secret store. Developers read secrets there with the native Google SDK.
signs: Your apps already read secrets from GCP Secret Manager.
You want PAM rotation and audit without changing those apps.

k8s_openshift.what: Red Hat OpenShift clusters. They use the same Kubernetes integrations.
signs: You deploy apps on OpenShift.
Pods need credentials for databases or APIs.

k8s_other.what: Any other Kubernetes distribution you manage yourself.
signs: You run self-managed Kubernetes clusters.
Pods need credentials for databases or APIs.

op_linux.what: Linux servers and VMs in your data center.
signs: Scripts, cron jobs or services read passwords from files.
You want servers to authenticate without a stored password.

op_windows.what: Windows servers in your data center.
signs: Services or scheduled tasks use stored passwords.
Windows apps keep credentials in config files.

op_appservers.what: Java application servers that keep data source passwords in their configuration.
signs: Data sources in Tomcat, JBoss, WebSphere or WebLogic hold passwords.
You want the app server to fetch them from PAM.

op_legacy.what: Packaged or legacy applications you cannot easily change.
signs: The app reads a password from a file, registry or database table.
Changing the app code is hard or not allowed.

op_cf.what: Cloud Foundry or VMware Tanzu Application Service platforms.
signs: You push apps to Cloud Foundry or Tanzu.
Apps get credentials from service bindings or manifests.
Apps connect with a shared database password.
Rotating that password breaks apps or needs a maintenance window.

op_hcv.what: HashiCorp Vault, Open Source or Enterprise, already used by developers.
signs: Developers read secrets from HashiCorp Vault.
You want PAM rotation and audit for those secrets.

op_iot.what: Devices in the field that connect to your services.
signs: Devices carry passwords, keys or certificates.
You want devices to authenticate without a shared password.

mf_zos.what: Batch jobs and programs on IBM z/OS that need passwords at run time.
signs: JCL jobs pass passwords in datasets or members.
You want z/OS to fetch them from PAM with a local cache.

ci_jenkins.what: Jenkins pipelines that need secrets during builds and deployments.
signs: Your pipelines run in Jenkins.
Secrets live in CI variables, credentials stores or the repository.

ci_gitlab.what: GitLab CI/CD pipelines that need secrets during builds and deployments.
signs: Your pipelines run in GitLab CI/CD.
Secrets live in CI variables, credentials stores or the repository.

ci_gha.what: GitHub Actions pipelines that need secrets during builds and deployments.
signs: Your pipelines run in GitHub Actions.
Secrets live in CI variables, credentials stores or the repository.

ci_bitbucket.what: Bitbucket Pipelines pipelines that need secrets during builds and deployments.
signs: Your pipelines run in Bitbucket Pipelines.
Secrets live in CI variables, credentials stores or the repository.

ci_circleci.what: CircleCI pipelines that need secrets during builds and deployments.
signs: Your pipelines run in CircleCI.
Secrets live in CI variables, credentials stores or the repository.

ci_octopus.what: Octopus Deploy pipelines that need secrets during builds and deployments.
signs: Your pipelines run in Octopus Deploy.
Secrets live in CI variables, credentials stores or the repository.

ci_ansible.what: Playbooks that log in to servers and devices.
signs: You automate with Ansible.
Credentials sit in variables, vaults or files next to the code.

ci_terraform.what: Infrastructure as code that needs provider and database credentials.
signs: You automate with Terraform.
Credentials sit in variables, vaults or files next to the code.

ci_puppet.what: Configuration management that applies settings with credentials on each node.
signs: You automate with Puppet.
Credentials sit in variables, vaults or files next to the code.

ai_agents.what: AI agents that call APIs and services on their own.
signs: Your agents use long-lived API keys.
You want each agent to have its own short-lived identity.

ai_mcp.what: AI coding assistants that work with secrets through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).
signs: Developers use AI tools while writing code.
You want the assistant to create secrets in the vault instead of in code.
Your privileged accounts are in Privilege Cloud.
The CPM rotates them from your connectors.

pam_sh.what: PAM installed and operated in your own environment (Digital Vault, PVWA, CPM).
signs: Your privileged accounts are in your own Digital Vault.
Your team runs the PAM servers.
Your services are written in Java / Spring.
They read secrets from config files or environment variables.
Your services are written in .NET.
They read secrets from config files or environment variables.
Your services are written in Python.
They read secrets from config files or environment variables.
You build integrations on MuleSoft.
Mule apps keep credentials in properties.

g_unsure.what: We pick the goals from what you selected in steps 1 and 2.
signs: You want a first recommendation quickly.
You will refine the goals later with the team.

g_hardcoded.what: Apps, scripts and pipelines fetch secrets at run time with their own identity, so nothing stays in code, images or config.
signs: Passwords or tokens appear in repositories, images or CI variables.
Teams copy the same secret to many places.

g_vault_gov.what: Keep the cloud secret stores developers already use, with rotation, policy and audit coming from PAM.
signs: Each cloud team runs its own secret store.
Security has no central view of rotation and access.

g_legacy_pam.what: Servers, app servers, legacy apps and mainframe jobs fetch privileged accounts from PAM at run time instead of storing them.
signs: Privileged passwords sit in config files of servers or apps.
You already rotate those accounts in PAM, but apps break.

g_workload_id.what: Workloads get short-lived SPIFFE identities (SVIDs) and use them for mTLS between services, cloud federation or secret exchange.
signs: Services talk to each other and need mutual trust.
You want workloads to reach cloud APIs without static keys.

g_ai.what: AI agents and AI tools work without long-lived keys in code or configuration.
signs: Agents hold API keys to call models or services.
AI assistants could write secrets into code.

g_dynamic.what: Cloud credentials created on demand with a time to live, which expire on their own.
signs: Long-lived cloud access keys are shared across teams.
You want access that disappears after the job.

g_rotation.what: Rotate passwords on a schedule without breaking the applications that use them.
signs: Password changes cause outages or need a maintenance window.
Some passwords have not changed in years.

g_audit.what: Know which workload or person accessed which secret, when, and send those events to your SIEM.
signs: Auditors ask who used a credential.
You need machine access events in the SIEM.

cmp.title: Compare products, use cases and technologies
cmp.subtitle: Start with the four products side by side, then pick one product to compare its use cases and technologies on the same dimensions: identity, delivery, code changes, rotation, availability and limits.
cmp.glance_lead: What each product solves, who consumes it and where the credential lives. Select a product name to open its overview.

sm.problem: Secrets hardcoded in code, images, config files and pipelines.
sm.consumer: Workloads: applications, pods, pipelines, scripts and AI coding tools.
sm.identity: The workload proves who it is with a native identity (Kubernetes JWT, cloud IAM, CI OIDC token, certificate) or an API key; policy decides what it can read.
sm.where: In Secrets Manager, either stored there or synced from PAM Safes (data/vault).
sm.usecases: Kubernetes, CI/CD, platforms, Summon, dynamic secrets, certificates (SaaS).
sm.choose: Applications and pipelines need secrets at run time without storing them.

swa.problem: Workloads that share static secrets to prove who they are.
swa.consumer: Workloads on Kubernetes, VMs and cloud, and AI agents.
swa.identity: SPIFFE IDs: X.509-SVID and JWT-SVID issued after attestation by the SWA Agent and renewed before they expire.
swa.where: No stored credential: short-lived SVIDs. A JWT-SVID can be exchanged for secrets in Secrets Manager or for cloud credentials.
swa.editions: A feature of Secrets Manager SaaS, US-EAST-1 region only.
swa.usecases: Service-to-service mTLS, cloud federation (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud), secret exchange, AI agents.
swa.choose: The target can verify SPIFFE or OIDC tokens and you want to remove the secret zero.

cp.problem: Privileged account passwords hardcoded in applications, application servers, scripts and mainframe jobs.
cp.consumer: Applications on their servers, application servers (JDBC), remote scripts and z/OS jobs.
cp.identity: An application ID (AppID) plus registered characteristics: allowed machines, OS user, path, hash or client certificate.
cp.where: In Vault Safes, rotated by the CPM and kept in an encrypted local cache.
cp.usecases: Credential Provider, ASCP, Central Credential Provider, z/OS, Dual Accounts.
cp.choose: Traditional applications that use privileged accounts managed in PAM.

shub.problem: Secrets spread across cloud stores with no central rotation policy or audit.
shub.consumer: Applications that read AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager or HashiCorp Vault natively.
shub.identity: Applications keep their cloud identity. Secrets Hub writes to each store with an IAM role, federated identity, Workload Identity Federation or a JWT/OIDC role.
shub.where: The source of truth is a PAM Safe; the target stores hold synced copies (one-way sync).
shub.editions: SaaS service. Source: Privilege Cloud or PAM Self-Hosted 11.5 or later (through a connector).
shub.usecases: Sync PAM secrets to cloud stores; discover and review the secrets already in those stores.
shub.choose: Developers must keep native cloud SDK calls while security keeps rotation and audit in PAM.

cmp.detail_lead: Pick a product, then a category. Every column links to its page; the rows are the same everywhere so you can compare.

cat_lead.k8s: Ways to get secrets into pods: from the application itself to operators, drivers and brokers that need no code.
cat_lead.cicd: Pipelines and infrastructure tools. Most use a short-lived JWT from the CI platform instead of a stored key.
cat_lead.platforms: Language SDKs and platforms outside Kubernetes.
cat_lead.tools: Cross-cutting tools and capabilities of Secrets Manager.
cat_lead.swa: What a workload can do with its SPIFFE identity. See the SWA architecture page for the components.
cat_lead.cp: All providers use the same Vault, application definitions and Safe permissions. They differ in where the provider runs and how the application calls it.
cat_lead.sources: Where the secrets come from. The target stores and the application side are the same for both.
cat_lead.targets: Where Secrets Hub writes. Applications keep their native calls.

rows.delivery: How the secret reaches the workload

cmp.shub_limits_title: Integration limitations that apply to every target
shub_limits: Keys and certificates are not supported, only secrets. Dual accounts are not supported.
One-way sync: manual changes in a target are not detected and can be overwritten.
Up to 10,000 accounts synced per tenant and up to 1,000 sync policies.
cmp.source_note: Values summarize each linked page, which cites the official documentation. Not documented means the documentation does not state it.

sdk.name: SDK (Spring Boot)
sdk.identity: Pod ServiceAccount JWT sent to authn-jwt.
sdk.delivery: The app calls the REST API and keeps values in memory (5 minute cache in the demo).
sdk.code: Yes: SDK or REST calls in the application.
sdk.rotation: Next fetch after the cache expires; no restart.
sdk.best: Java services that want control and per-secret audit.

sidecar.name: Sidecar (.NET)
sidecar.identity: Pod ServiceAccount JWT, presented by the Secrets Provider sidecar.
sidecar.delivery: The sidecar writes a Kubernetes Secret; the app reads environment variables (secretKeyRef).
sidecar.rotation: The sidecar keeps the Secret updated; environment variables need a restart (Reloader).
sidecar.limit: Values also exist as a Kubernetes Secret object.
sidecar.best: Polyglot apps that must not change code.

eso.name: External Secrets Operator
eso.identity: ServiceAccount JWT (audience conjur) used by the SecretStore.
eso.delivery: ExternalSecret syncs into a Kubernetes Secret; pods load it with envFrom.
eso.rotation: Refresh every minute in the demo; environment variables need a rolling restart.
eso.limit: The value is stored as a Kubernetes Secret.

csi.name: CSI Driver
csi.identity: Projected ServiceAccount token (audience conjur) used by the provider.
csi.delivery: Files on a read-only tmpfs volume; no Kubernetes Secret.
csi.code: Read files from the mount path.
csi.rotation: The rotation reconciler rewrites the volume (every 2 minutes in the demo); no restart.
csi.limit: The app must read files, not environment variables.

spmodes.name: Secrets Provider modes
spmodes.identity: authn-jwt, authn-iam, authn-azure, authn-gcp; Self-Hosted adds authn-k8s.
spmodes.delivery: Kubernetes Secrets or Push-to-File; init container, sidecar, Job or standalone.
spmodes.rotation: Only the sidecar and standalone update after start.
spmodes.limit: Push-to-File only with init container and sidecar; fetch all is capped at 500 secrets.
spmodes.best: Choosing the right deployment for each app.

reloader.name: Reloader
reloader.identity: Does not talk to Secrets Manager; watches Kubernetes Secrets.
reloader.delivery: Rolls the Deployments and StatefulSets that reference a changed Secret.
reloader.rotation: Automatic rollout when the Secret changes.
reloader.limit: Needs the Secrets Provider Helm chart in application or standalone mode.
reloader.best: Apps reading environment variables that must pick up rotated values.

secretless.name: Secretless Broker
secretless.identity: authn-k8s with a Follower in the cluster.
secretless.delivery: The app connects to a local broker, which adds the credential to the connection.
secretless.code: Point the connection at localhost, with no credentials.
secretless.rotation: The broker uses current values; no restart.
secretless.limit: Self-Hosted only; supported protocols only (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MSSQL, SSH, HTTP).
secretless.best: Apps that must never see the password.

gha.name: GitHub Actions
gha.identity: GitHub OIDC JWT bound to repository and workflow.
gha.delivery: The action fetches values as environment variables masked in logs.
gha.code: One workflow step plus permissions id-token: write.
gha.rotation: Each run fetches the current value.
gha.limit: Any repository or workflow that does not match the host annotations is denied.
gha.best: GitHub pipelines with no stored credential.

jenkins.name: Jenkins
jenkins.identity: A 2 minute JWT signed by Jenkins, verified through its JWKS endpoint.
jenkins.delivery: The plugin injects environment variables inside withCredentials, masked in logs.
jenkins.code: withCredentials with credential IDs in the Jenkinsfile.
jenkins.rotation: Each build fetches the current value.
jenkins.limit: Plugin v3.x requires Jenkins 2.455 or later.
jenkins.best: Jenkins pipelines with Global, Folder or Job credentials.

ansible.name: Ansible
ansible.identity: JWT from your IdP; API key, AWS IAM, Azure and GCP are also supported.
ansible.delivery: The lookup plugin resolves the value at play time on the control node.
ansible.rotation: Each run reads the current value.
ansible.limit: Tasks need no_log: true, or values can appear in output.

terraform.name: Terraform
terraform.identity: Provider authentication, for example JWT or API key (host_id when required).
terraform.delivery: Data sources or ephemeral resources read inside the manifest.
terraform.limit: Values are written to state unless ephemeral (1.10+) or write-only (1.11+).
terraform.best: Infrastructure pipelines, and managing Secrets Manager as code.

gitlab.name: GitLab CI/CD
gitlab.identity: GitLab ID token (JWT) whose aud matches the authenticator.
gitlab.delivery: A binary prints each secret to STDOUT and the script captures it.
gitlab.code: One call per CONJUR_SECRET_ID in the job script.
gitlab.rotation: Each job fetches the current value.
gitlab.limit: Images only for Alpine, Ubuntu and UBI-FIPS; one call per secret.
gitlab.best: GitLab pipelines tied to project and branch.

azdo.name: Azure DevOps
azdo.identity: Entra ID token through an Azure Resource Manager service connection (JWT); API key also supported.
azdo.delivery: A batch of secrets from secrets.yml becomes environment variables.
azdo.rotation: Each run fetches the current value.
azdo.limit: Read only: it cannot create, update or remove secrets.
azdo.best: Azure Pipelines that already have an Azure identity.

bitbucket.name: Bitbucket Pipelines
bitbucket.identity: Bitbucket OIDC JWT per step; the workload is the repository UUID.
bitbucket.delivery: Written to secrets.env and exported by load_secrets.sh.
bitbucket.code: Add the pipe to the step.
bitbucket.rotation: Each run fetches the current value.
bitbucket.limit: The file is readable by every process in the step; only _ is allowed as a special character.

circleci.name: CircleCI
circleci.identity: CircleCI OIDC token signed for your organization.
circleci.delivery: The orb exports the listed secrets as environment variables.
circleci.rotation: Each job fetches the current value.
circleci.limit: The audience must be your CircleCI organization ID.
circleci.best: CircleCI projects that should stop storing secrets in contexts.

octopus.name: Octopus Deploy
octopus.identity: JWT from a Generic OIDC account (audience conjur).
octopus.delivery: Each secret becomes an output variable for the next steps.
octopus.rotation: Each deployment fetches the current value.
octopus.limit: One missing or inaccessible secret fails the whole step (SaaS guide).

python.name: Python and AWS Lambda
python.identity: SDK: API key on SaaS; Self-Hosted also LDAP and JWT. AWS IAM client: the instance IAM role.
python.delivery: The SDK returns values to the code (get, get_many).
python.limit: The IAM client token is not refreshed (5 to 8 minutes) and is read only.
python.best: Python on EC2 with no secret zero, and automation.

cf.name: Cloud Foundry / Tanzu
cf.identity: The Service Broker creates one host per app or per space.
cf.delivery: A buildpack (Summon) injects environment variables at start.
cf.rotation: Only after a restart or restage.
cf.limit: Self-Hosted only; one service instance per space.
cf.best: Tanzu Application Service and Cloud Foundry apps.

puppet.name: Puppet
puppet.identity: A host API key on each node.
puppet.delivery: The agent fetches at apply time with Deferred functions.
puppet.code: Use the module function in manifests.
puppet.rotation: Fetched again on each agent run (Deferred).
puppet.limit: Self-Hosted only; the node API key is a secret zero.

mulesoft.name: MuleSoft
mulesoft.delivery: The Retrieve secret operation inside a Mule flow.
mulesoft.code: Add the operation in Anypoint Studio.
mulesoft.limit: Read only, and the API key is a secret zero.
mulesoft.best: Mule integrations that keep credentials in properties files today.

summon.name: Summon
summon.identity: Uses an identity already configured on the machine.
summon.delivery: Environment variables or temporary files for a child process.
summon.rotation: Read once at start; a restart picks up the new value.
summon.limit: Environment variables are visible on the host.
summon.best: Legacy scripts, systemd services and Terraform via Summon.

mcp.name: MCP Server
mcp.identity: The developer signs in through Idira Identity OAuth2; the agent acts as that user.
mcp.delivery: The AI tool creates secrets and workloads and generates code that fetches them.
mcp.code: Generated SDK calls replace the literals.
mcp.rotation: Not applicable: the generated code fetches at run time.
mcp.limit: Beta, development only; no boundary between the agent and the user.
mcp.best: Moving hardcoded secrets out of code with an AI tool.

dynamic.name: Dynamic secrets
dynamic.identity: Any authenticator; the workload must be in the issuer consumers group.
dynamic.delivery: Each read creates a new AWS or GCP credential.
dynamic.rotation: Nothing to rotate: it expires after its TTL (15 minutes to 12 hours).
dynamic.limit: Cloud targets only: AWS on both editions, GCP on SaaS.
dynamic.best: Short-lived cloud access for jobs and workloads.

certs.name: Certificates
certs.identity: The workload must be in the issuer executors group.
certs.delivery: Issue (certificate and key) or sign (CSR only) through Certificate Manager.
certs.limit: SaaS only, with Certificate Manager as the back end.

mtls.name: X.509-SVID (mTLS)
mtls.identity: Attestation by the SWA Agent (k8s_psat, x509pop or AWS instance identity).
mtls.delivery: The Workload API on a local socket returns the X.509-SVID and the trust bundle.
mtls.rotation: The agent renews the SVID before it expires; no restart.
mtls.limit: TCP 8443 to the SWA Server must be reachable from every node.

jwtsm.name: JWT-SVID to Secrets Manager
jwtsm.identity: An RSA-signed JWT-SVID sent to the Secrets Manager JWT authenticator.
jwtsm.delivery: Exchanged for an access token; the workload reads only the secrets policy grants.
jwtsm.code: Fetch the SVID, then call the REST API.
jwtsm.rotation: SVIDs renew automatically; secrets are read at request time.
jwtsm.limit: RSA signatures only; new identities have no secret access until granted.
jwtsm.best: Targets that are not SPIFFE-aware and still need a password.

aws.name: SVID to AWS (S3 demo)
aws.delivery: The cloud returns temporary credentials (OIDC federation).
aws.rotation: Temporary credentials expire; a new SVID gets new ones.
aws.limit: The issuer URL must be public, unauthenticated HTTPS.

ai.name: AI agents
ai.identity: Attestation, then one JWT-SVID per audience.
ai.delivery: Secrets from Secrets Manager, a Claude API token, Gemini Enterprise (agentless flow).
ai.code: SDK federation settings; no API key in the code.
ai.rotation: Tokens are minted on demand and expire in minutes.
ai.limit: US-EAST-1 only; Claude API federation accepts JWT-SVIDs only.
ai.best: AI agents that should hold no API key.

cp.name: Credential Provider (CP)
cp.identity: AppID plus allowed machines, OS user, path and hash.
cp.delivery: A local SDK (Java, .NET, C/C++, CLI) answers from an encrypted cache.
cp.rotation: The background cache refresh picks up CPM changes.
cp.limit: An agent on every server; up to 10 applications per CP recommended.

ascp.name: Application Server CP (ASCP)
ascp.identity: Allowed machines, OS user, path and hash (no client certificate).
ascp.delivery: The JDBC driver proxy gets the credential for the data source.
ascp.code: None: a data source configuration change.
ascp.rotation: New connections use it after the next cache refresh.
ascp.limit: Supported application servers and databases only; JRE 1.8 or later.
ascp.best: WebSphere, WebLogic, JBoss and Tomcat data sources.

ccp.name: Central Credential Provider (CCP)
ccp.identity: AppID plus allowed machines, Windows OS user (IIS) or client certificate.
ccp.rotation: Background cache refresh (25 minutes by default) and CPM change notification.
ccp.limit: Windows IIS only; one password per call.
ccp.best: Applications where no agent can be installed.

zos.name: Credential Provider for z/OS
zos.identity: AppID plus allowed machines and OS user.
zos.delivery: The JCL SDK writes the password to CREDOUT, or the C/C++ SDK returns it.
zos.code: A JCL step or SDK call.
zos.rotation: The CPM marks the password and the provider reads it again; cache refresh every 180 seconds.
zos.limit: One provider per LPAR; z/OS 2.5, 3.1 or 3.2.

dual.name: Dual Accounts
dual.identity: Consumers query the VirtualUserName, not a specific account.
dual.delivery: Always returns the Active account, through a Credential Provider or Secrets Manager.
dual.rotation: The CPM changes only the inactive account, after the GracePeriod.
dual.limit: Rotation by the CPM only; GracePeriod must cover every consumer refresh.
dual.best: High load, critical apps that need rotation with no downtime.

src_pc.name: Privilege Cloud (SaaS)
src_pc.identity: The SecretsHub user is a member of each Safe to sync.
src_pc.delivery: Sync policies map Safes to target stores.
src_pc.rotation: Each CPM rotation is synced to every target.
src_pc.limit: SecretsHub user in up to 1,000 Safes; up to 1,000 accounts per Safe.
src_pc.best: Privilege Cloud Standalone and Shared Services customers.

src_pamsh.name: PAM Self-Hosted
src_pamsh.identity: The SecretsHub user (DAPService) in the Vault; a connector reaches PVWA.
src_pamsh.delivery: The connector reads accounts from PVWA over HTTPS; Secrets Hub writes them.
src_pamsh.rotation: Same path on each CPM rotation.
src_pamsh.limit: PAM 11.5 or later, a connector is always required, one load balancer in front of PVWA.

t_aws.name: AWS Secrets Manager
t_aws.identity: An IAM role that Secrets Hub assumes.
t_aws.limit: Names up to 512 characters; secrets managed by AWS cannot be changed.

t_azure.name: Azure Key Vault
t_azure.identity: An app registration with federated identity (no client secret).
t_azure.limit: Access policy model not supported (RBAC only); names up to 127 characters.

t_gcp.name: GCP Secret Manager
t_gcp.identity: Workload Identity Federation with a service account.
t_gcp.limit: Labels truncated to 63 characters; the replication policy cannot change later.

t_hcv.name: HashiCorp Vault
t_hcv.identity: A JWT/OIDC auth role; a connector is always required.
t_hcv.rotation: Synced after each CPM rotation, through the connector.
t_hcv.limit: KV version 2 only; the connector must sit in the Vault network.

cmp.finder_cta_desc: Select what your environment has and see which products and pages fit.

vault.title: Vault Info
vault.subtitle: The accounts in the demo Safe, explained field by field, with CPM rotation and version history. Whoever runs the demo never opens the Vault: this page consumes it securely through Secrets Manager.
vault.chain_title: How this page reaches the Vault
vault.chain_lead: No static secret: the backend proves its own identity and receives the API credential at the moment of use.
vault.chain_conjur_jwt_desc: The pod presents its service account JWT (audience conjur) to the Secrets Manager authn-jwt authenticator.
vault.chain_conjur_secret_desc: With the access token it reads {{account}}, synced from the {{safe}} Safe to data/vault.
vault.chain_identity_token_desc: Exchanges the credential for a short-lived OAuth token (client credentials).
vault.chain_privilege_cloud_desc: Queries Privilege Cloud, only in the {{safe}} Safe.
vault.search: Search by name, user, address or platform
vault.pick_desc: See what each field means, the version history, and request a password rotation.
vault.detail_lead: Account metadata in the Vault. The secret value is never shown.
vault.f_safe_help: Logical vault that groups the accounts and defines who can do what (members and permissions).
vault.f_platform_help: Defines how the CPM connects to, verifies and changes this credential (rotation policy and plugin).
vault.f_user_help: Credential user name on the target system.
vault.f_address_help: Host, database or service where the credential is used.
vault.f_auto_on_help: The CPM changes and verifies the password on its own, following the platform policy.
vault.f_auto_off_help: The CPM does not change this credential on its own; changes are manual or done by another process.
vault.f_status_help: Result of the last management action (change, verify or reconcile).
vault.f_changed_help: When the credential value last changed.
vault.f_verified_help: When the CPM confirmed that the Vault value works on the target.
vault.f_reconciled_help: When the CPM fixed a mismatch using a reconcile account.
vault.f_conjur_help: Variable synced by the Vault Synchronizer: applications read from here without reaching the Vault.
vault.dual_desc: Two accounts on the target form a pair with the same virtual name. While one is in use (current), the CPM changes the other's password; on the next change the roles swap. Applications never use a password mid-change: zero-downtime rotation.
vault.hist_lead: The current version and the two before it. The value is always masked; the page does not even read the secret, only the version metadata.
vault.rot_lead: Asks the CPM to change the password now. The new version shows in the history and reaches Conjur on the next sync cycle.
vault.rot_sensitive: {{name}} grants access to infrastructure, cloud or the platform itself. Rotating it in the middle of a demo can interrupt whoever uses this credential.
vault.rot_sending: Sending the request to the Vault…
vault.rot_waiting: Request accepted. Waiting for the CPM to finish…
vault.rot_wait: Wait one minute between rotation requests.
vault.rot_self: This is the credential the page itself uses: its rotation stays in the Vault, so the tool does not switch itself off in the middle of a demo.
vault.rot_cpm_failed: The CPM reported a failure. Check the last operation status.
vault.rot_timeout: The CPM did not finish within 3 minutes; the change may complete later. Refresh the account to check.
vault.footnote: vault-control backend on EKS: authenticates to Secrets Manager only with the service account JWT (no API key), reads the Vault credential at the moment of use and never retrieves the value of the accounts shown.
